independent_reader: Six separate AI-assisted readers (Claude) compared every drafted pair against the complete source and target texts; none drafted the pairs they read.

findings.finding: Revelation 1:1 does not explicitly say the angel was sent by Jesus; the subject “He” of “made it known” is not named, so the claim that both verses describe an angel sent by Jesus goes beyond the shown text.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both verses describe the revelation as delivered through an angel sent by Jesus: “I, Jesus, sent My angel to testify these things.” Revelation 22:16 restates in Jesus’ own voice the chain of transmission set out in the opening verse.
findings.after: Both verses describe the revelation as delivered through an angel: in 1:1 it is made known “by sending through His angel to His slave John,” and in 22:16 Jesus says, “I, Jesus, sent My angel to testify these things to you for the Churches.” Revelation 22:16 restates in Jesus’ own voice the chain of transmission set out in the opening verse.

findings.finding: Revelation 1:9 does not present the word of God and testimony of Jesus as the content of John’s witness, only as the reason he was on Patmos.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both verses join “the word of God” and “the testimony of Jesus” as the content of John’s witness. Revelation 1:9 gives this pairing as the reason John was on Patmos.
findings.after: Both verses join “the word of God” and “the testimony of Jesus”: in 1:2 as what John testified to, and in 1:9 as the reason John came to be on Patmos.

findings.finding: The threefold title is not inside the Lord God’s quoted words in 1:8; it describes the speaker, so ‘places it on the lips of the Lord God’ is inaccurate.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both use the identical threefold title “the One who is and who was and who is coming.” Revelation 1:8 places it on the lips of the Lord God together with “the Alpha and the Omega” and “the Almighty.”
findings.after: Both use the identical threefold title “the One who is and who was and who is coming.” Revelation 1:8 applies it to the Lord God, who says “I am the Alpha and the Omega,” and adds “the Almighty.”

findings.finding: The shown Psalm verse does not call the recipient an ‘anointed king’; that detail comes from outside the passage.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: The Psalm promises to make the anointed king “firstborn, high among the kings of the earth,” and Revelation calls Jesus “the firstborn of the dead and the ruler of the kings of the earth.” Revelation adds “of the dead,” applying the title to resurrection.
findings.after: The Psalm promises, “I will make him firstborn, high among the kings of the earth,” and Revelation calls Jesus “the firstborn of the dead and the ruler of the kings of the earth.” Revelation adds “of the dead,” applying the title to resurrection.

findings.finding: Revelation 5:10 as shown does not mention the Lamb or a song to the Lamb, nor does it name Christ as the one who made them a kingdom; it addresses “Thou.”
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both say that Christ has made His people “a kingdom” and “priests” to God. Revelation 5:10 sets this in the song to the Lamb and adds that “they shall reign upon the earth.”
findings.after: Both say that God’s people have been made “a kingdom” and “priests” to God (1:6 “made us a kingdom, priests”; 5:10 “Thou didst make them a kingdom and priests”). Revelation 5:10 says this in an address to “Thou” and adds that “they shall reign upon the earth.”

findings.finding: Neither Sinai nor ‘those freed by Christ’s blood’ appears in the shown verses (the latter is from Revelation 1:5, not the source 1:6).
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: At Sinai God tells Israel, “you shall be to Me a royal priesthood and a holy nation,” the background for Revelation’s “a kingdom, priests.” Exodus addresses the sons of Israel; Revelation applies the status to those freed by Christ’s blood.
findings.after: God’s words for the sons of Israel, “you shall be to Me a royal priesthood and a holy nation,” stand behind Revelation’s “a kingdom, priests.” Exodus addresses the sons of Israel; Revelation applies the status to “us,” made a kingdom and priests to His God and Father.

findings.finding: ‘The One who loves us and freed us’ comes from Revelation 1:5, not the shown source verse; and 1 Peter’s ‘to whom’ is not unambiguously God.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both close with an ascription of “the glory and the dominion” forever, ending in “Amen.” Peter directs it to God through Jesus Christ, while Revelation directs it to the One who loves us and freed us.
findings.after: Both close with an ascription of “the glory and the dominion” forever, ending in “Amen.” Peter’s ascription follows “so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ,” while Revelation’s is addressed “to Him” who made us a kingdom, priests to His God and Father.

findings.finding: Revelation 1:7 says “with the clouds,” not “upon the clouds”; the quoted phrase is only in Matthew, so ‘both combine the coming “upon the clouds”’ misquotes Revelation.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both combine the coming “upon the clouds” with the statement that “all the tribes of the earth will mourn.” Matthew speaks of “the Son of Man” and “the sign” in heaven; Revelation adds “those who pierced Him.”
findings.after: Both combine His coming on the clouds (Revelation “with the clouds”; Matthew “upon the clouds of heaven”) with His being seen and the statement that “all the tribes of the earth will mourn.” Matthew speaks of “the Son of Man” and “the sign” in heaven; Revelation adds “those who pierced Him.”

findings.finding: Revelation 1:9 does not identify John’s witness with the pair; it gives the pair as the reason he was on Patmos, so ‘Both verses identify John’s witness’ overstates 1:9.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both verses identify John’s witness with “the word of God” and “the testimony of Jesus.” Revelation 1:2 describes what John testified to; 1:9 gives the same pair as the reason he was on Patmos.
findings.after: Both verses join “the word of God” and “the testimony of Jesus”: Revelation 1:2 describes them as what John testified to, and 1:9 gives the same pair as the reason he was on Patmos.

findings.finding: The shown Isaiah verse does not identify the speaker as ‘the servant’; that detail comes from outside the passage.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: The servant says God “made my mouth like a sharp sword,” the image behind the sword coming from Christ’s mouth. In Isaiah the mouth is compared to a sword; in Revelation a sword comes out of it.
findings.after: The speaker in Isaiah says that God “made my mouth like a sharp sword,” the image behind the sharp two-edged sword coming from His mouth in Revelation. In Isaiah the mouth is compared to a sword; in Revelation a sword comes out of it.

findings.finding: Revelation 19:15 does not carry out the war threatened in 2:16: 2:16 is directed against “them” in Pergamum, while 19:15 strikes the nations.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: In Revelation 19:15 “from His mouth cometh out a sharp sword” to strike the nations, carrying out the war with the sword of His mouth threatened here.
findings.after: In Revelation 19:15 “from His mouth cometh out a sharp sword, so that with it He may strike the nations,” the same image of judgment with the sword of His mouth threatened here. In 2:16 the threat concerns those in Pergamum; in 19:15 the sword strikes the nations.

findings.finding: The shown Isaiah verse does not call the figure a king, and “the breath of his lips” misquotes “breath through his lips.”
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Isaiah’s king will “strike the earth with the word of his mouth” and slay the ungodly with the breath of his lips, the background for judgment by what comes from the mouth. Isaiah does not speak of a sword.
findings.after: The figure in Isaiah will “strike the earth with the word of his mouth,” and “with breath through his lips he will slay the ungodly,” the background for judgment by what comes from the mouth. Isaiah does not speak of a sword.

findings.finding: The shown Isaiah verse does not name Zion as the addressee.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Isaiah promises, “He will call you your new name, which the Lord will name,” comparable to the “new name written” given to the conqueror. Isaiah addresses Zion; Revelation an individual conqueror, with the name on a white stone.
findings.after: Isaiah promises, “He will call you your new name, which the Lord will name,” comparable to the “new name written” given to the conqueror. Isaiah addresses a “you” whose righteousness the nations will see; Revelation an individual conqueror, with the name on a white stone.

findings.finding: ‘Anointed king’ and ‘risen Christ’ are not in the shown texts; the rationale also contains stray punctuation (“letter,.”).
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: The Psalm’s decree, “You are My son,” lies behind the title “the Son of God” used in this letter,. The Psalm addresses the anointed king, while Revelation uses the title of the risen Christ.
findings.after: The Psalm’s decree, “You are My son,” lies behind the title “the Son of God” used in this letter. In the Psalm the Lord says this to the speaker; in Revelation the title introduces the One who speaks to Thyatira.

findings.finding: The shown verse does not name Ahab or call Jezebel a queen; it says only that “he took as wife Jezebel.”
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Ahab took as wife “Jezebel” and served Baal, the queen whose name is given to the false prophetess at Thyatira. Kings does not call Jezebel a prophetess.
findings.after: In Kings “he took as wife Jezebel daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians” and served Baal; her name is the one given to the false prophetess at Thyatira. Kings does not call Jezebel a prophetess.

findings.finding: The shown Ezekiel text does not call the addressee a city, and in Ezekiel the lovers are gathered against the adulteress as agents of punishment rather than sharing in the judgment.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: God gathers against the unfaithful city “all your lovers” and exacts “the retribution of an adulteress,” paralleling judgment falling on the adulteress and her partners.
findings.after: God gathers against the unfaithful one “all your lovers” and will exact “the retribution of an adulteress,” comparable to the judgment on Jezebel and those committing adultery with her. In Ezekiel the lovers are gathered as agents of the punishment, whereas in Revelation those committing adultery with her share in the affliction.

findings.finding: Revelation 18:9 as shown does not name Babylon, and it speaks of the kings mourning over her rather than of affliction imposed on them.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: The kings who “committed sexual immorality” with Babylon will weep and mourn over her, comparable to the great affliction for those committing adultery with Jezebel.
findings.after: The kings of the earth who “committed sexual immorality and lived in luxury with her” will “weep and mourn over her” when they see her burning; as in 2:22, those who shared a woman’s immorality are caught up in grief at her judgment. Revelation 18:9 does not name the woman and speaks of mourning rather than of affliction imposed on them.

findings.finding: Acts 15:28 as shown says “the Holy Spirit and to us”; ‘the apostles’ is not in the shown text.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: The Jerusalem letter says “to place no further burden upon you,” close to “I place no other burden upon you.” Acts attributes the decision to the Holy Spirit and the apostles, while Revelation gives it as Christ’s word.
findings.after: The Jerusalem letter says “to place no further burden upon you,” close to “I place no other burden upon you.” Acts attributes the decision to “the Holy Spirit and to us,” while in Revelation the speaker says, “I say.”

findings.finding: The shown Psalm verse does not identify the recipient as ‘the anointed son.’
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: The Psalm’s promise, “I will give you nations as your inheritance,” lies behind “I will give authority over the nations.” In the Psalm the promise is to the anointed son; Revelation extends it to the conqueror.
findings.after: The Psalm’s promise, “I will give you nations as your inheritance,” lies behind “I will give authority over the nations.” In the Psalm the promise is made to the one addressed as “you”; Revelation extends it to the conqueror.

findings.finding: The shown Psalm 2:8–9 does not identify the recipient as ‘the anointed son.’
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Revelation quotes Psalm 2:9: “You will shepherd them with an iron rod; you will crush them like a potter’s vessel.” Revelation applies to the conqueror the promise made in the Psalm to the anointed son.
findings.after: Revelation quotes Psalm 2:9: “You will shepherd them with an iron rod; you will crush them like a potter’s vessel.” Revelation applies to the conqueror the promise made in the Psalm to the one who is given “nations as your inheritance.”

findings.finding: Revelation 12:5 as shown speaks of a male child, not ‘the Messiah,’ and no Psalm is shown in this pair.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: The male child born to the woman is “to shepherd all the nations with an iron rod,” the same Psalm phrase applied directly to the Messiah.
findings.after: The male child born to the woman is “to shepherd all the nations with an iron rod,” the same phrase used in 2:27 of the conqueror’s rule.

findings.finding: Revelation 19:15 as shown does not mention a rider.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: The rider of Revelation 19 “will shepherd them with an iron rod,” the same phrase used here of the conqueror’s rule.
findings.after: In Revelation 19:15 the One from whose mouth comes a sharp sword “will shepherd them with an iron rod,” the same phrase used here of the conqueror’s rule.

findings.finding: Revelation 3:2 says nothing about Christ’s sudden coming; both quoted phrases come from 16:15, so ‘Both call for watchfulness in view of Christ’s sudden coming’ is not true of 3:2.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both call for watchfulness in view of Christ’s sudden coming: “Blessed is the one who watcheth,” and “I am coming like a thief.” Revelation 16:15 adds keeping one’s garments, which the Sardis warning does not mention.
findings.after: Both call for watchfulness: Sardis is told, “Become watchful,” and Revelation 16:15 says, “Blessed is the one who watcheth.” Revelation 16:15 grounds this in “I am coming like a thief” and adds keeping one’s garments, which the Sardis verse does not mention.

findings.finding: Revelation 3:3 is a conditional warning (“if thou watch not”); it does not say the church does not watch.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both sayings have the Lord announcing that he will come “like a thief” and link this with watching. Revelation 16:15 adds a blessing on the one who keeps his garments, whereas the Sardis warning is addressed to a church that does not watch.
findings.after: Both sayings have the Lord announcing that he will come “like a thief” and link this with watching. Revelation 16:15 adds a blessing on the one who keeps his garments, whereas the Sardis warning is conditional: “if thou watch not.”

findings.finding: Revelation 3:4 does not use the phrase “white garments” or say they are given by the Lord; it says the few did not defile their garments and will walk with Him in white.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both speak of “white garments” given by the Lord to cover a person. Laodicea is counselled to buy them to hide its nakedness, whereas the few in Sardis are already said not to have defiled their garments.
findings.after: Both connect white clothing with standing before the Lord: the few in Sardis “did not defile their garments” and “shall walk with Me in white,” and Laodicea is counselled to buy from Him “white garments” so that “the shame of thy nakedness may not be manifested.”

findings.finding: The rationale itself admits the shown Greek-based Isaiah wording has no key and no opening or shutting, so the verbal overlap is minimal; the connection is background rather than verbal allusion in this wording.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both describe authority connected with David that cannot be opposed: Isaiah’s figure receives “David’s glory” and rules “with no one contradicting,” and Christ opens and “no one will shut.” The Saints (Greek) wording of Isaiah has “David’s glory” rather than a key and does not mention opening and shutting.
findings.after: Both describe authority connected with David that cannot be opposed: Isaiah’s figure receives “David’s glory” and rules “with no one contradicting,” and Christ opens and “no one will shut.” The Saints (Greek) wording of Isaiah has “David’s glory” rather than a key and does not mention opening and shutting.

findings.finding: John 17:6 as shown speaks of “the people whom Thou gavest Me,” not explicitly ‘disciples,’ and of “Thy name.”
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both commend those who have kept the word: Philadelphia “didst keep My word,” and Jesus says of his disciples, “they have kept Thy word,” in the context of revealing God’s name.
findings.after: Both commend those who have kept the word: Philadelphia “didst keep My word,” and Jesus says of the people the Father gave Him, “they have kept Thy word,” in the context of revealing “Thy name.”

findings.finding: The shown Isaiah verse does not name Zion.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both describe outsiders who will “bow” at the feet of God’s people, followed by recognition: Isaiah’s “You will know that I am the Lord” and Revelation’s “know that I loved thee.” In Isaiah it is kings and ruling women who bow to Zion.
findings.after: Both describe outsiders who will “bow” at the feet of those addressed, followed by recognition: Isaiah’s “You will know that I am the Lord” and Revelation’s “know that I loved thee.” In Isaiah it is kings and ruling women who bow and “lick the dust of your feet.”

findings.finding: Revelation 3:17 does not contain the words “become rich” (it has “I am rich and have become wealthy”), so ‘with the words “become rich”’ is inaccurate for both texts.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both expose a church’s complacency with the words “become rich”: Paul ironically says, “Already you have become rich!” to the Corinthians, and Laodicea says, “I… have become wealthy.”
findings.after: Both expose complacent self-assessment of wealth: Paul ironically tells the Corinthians, “Already you have become rich!” and Laodicea says, “I am rich and have become wealthy and need nothing.”

findings.finding: Revelation 3:20 does not say the Lord will 'remain' with him; it says He will come in and dine with him.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both promise that the Lord will come to the one who responds and remain with him: “I will come in unto him” and “We will come to him and make Our dwelling with him.”
findings.after: Both promise that the Lord will come to the one who responds and be with him: “I will come in unto him and dine with him” and “We will come to him and make Our dwelling with him.”

findings.finding: In the shown Revelation 2:7 the refrain does not close the letter; the conqueror promise follows it. 'Closes each of the seven letters' is false of the target.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both verses contain the identical refrain “Let the one who hath an ear hear what the Spirit saith to the Churches,” which closes each of the seven letters.
findings.after: Both verses contain the identical refrain “Let the one who hath an ear hear what the Spirit saith to the Churches,” which recurs in each of the seven letters. In Revelation 2:7 it is followed by the promise to the one who conquers.

findings.finding: Revelation 4:2 mentions no heavenly attendants, so 'Both describe … with heavenly attendants' is false; the 'confrontation with the king' is not in the shown text.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both describe a vision of the Lord “sitting on His throne” with heavenly attendants around him. Micaiah’s vision is reported in a prophetic confrontation with the king.
findings.after: Both describe a vision of the Lord “sitting on His throne.” Micaiah also sees “all the army of heaven” standing around Him on His right and His left; Revelation 4:2 shows only the throne and the One sitting upon it.

findings.finding: The shown Ezekiel 1:28 does not mention a throne; the bow-like brightness surrounds 'the likeness of the Lord’s glory'.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both surround the divine throne with a bow-like radiance: Ezekiel sees “the appearance of a bow when it is in the cloud” all around, and John “a rainbow around the throne.” Ezekiel does not compare it to an emerald.
findings.after: Both surround the divine presence with a bow-like radiance: Ezekiel sees “the appearance of a bow when it is in the cloud” in the brightness all around “the likeness of the Lord’s glory,” and John sees “a rainbow around the throne.” Ezekiel does not compare it to an emerald.

findings.finding: The quoted 'the One who… was and who is' misrepresents 11:17, which reads 'who is and who was'; the claim that 'who is coming' is omitted 'as God has now taken his power' is an interpretation not stated in the text.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both address God as “Lord God Almighty, the One who… was and who is.” Revelation 11:17 omits “who is coming,” as God has now taken his power and reigned.
findings.after: Both address God as “Lord God Almighty” followed by the title “the One who is and who was” (here in the order “who was and who is”). Revelation 11:17 lacks “who is coming” and gives thanks because God has “taken Thy great power and reigned.”

findings.finding: Daniel 12:7 calls the speaker 'the one clothed in fine linen', not an angelic figure.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both describe God as the one who lives for ever: Daniel’s angelic figure swears “by God who lives for ever,” and the living creatures honour “the One living for the ages of the ages.”
findings.after: Both describe God as the one who lives for ever: the one clothed in fine linen swears “by God who lives for ever,” and the living creatures honour “the One living for the ages of the ages.”

findings.finding: In 5:13 the praise comes from every creature, not only heavenly beings; in 4:9 'the ages of the ages' is part of God’s title, not the duration of the praise.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both describe heavenly beings giving honour and glory “to the One sitting upon the throne” for “the ages of the ages.” In Revelation 5:13 the praise is shared with the Lamb and is answered by the living creatures’ “Amen.”
findings.after: Both describe glory and honour given “to the One sitting upon the throne,” and both use the phrase “the ages of the ages” (in 4:9 as a title of God, in 5:13 for the duration of the praise). In Revelation 5:13 the praise comes from every creature, is shared with the Lamb, and is answered by the living creatures’ “Amen.”

findings.finding: Revelation 5:1 does not say the scroll cannot be read; that is stated only of Isaiah’s book.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both describe a sealed book that cannot be read: Isaiah’s “sealed book,” and the scroll “sealed with seven seals.”
findings.after: Both describe a sealed book: Isaiah’s “sealed book,” which the reader “cannot read, for it is sealed,” and the scroll “sealed with seven seals.”

findings.finding: 'Isaiah addresses spiritual blindness' is not in the shown text; Revelation 5:2 asks who is worthy rather than stating that no one can read the scroll.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both describe a sealed book that no one can read: in Isaiah one says, “I cannot read, for it is sealed.” Isaiah addresses spiritual blindness; Revelation asks who is worthy to open the scroll.
findings.after: Both concern a sealed book that must be opened: in Isaiah one says, “I cannot read, for it is sealed,” and the angel asks, “Who is worthy to open the scroll and loose its seals?”

findings.finding: Daniel 12:9 says 'the commands' are covered and sealed, not 'Daniel’s words'.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both describe revealed matters that remain closed to the seer: Daniel’s words are “covered and sealed,” and no one is found worthy to open John’s scroll. Daniel is told to go away, whereas John weeps.
findings.after: Both describe revealed matters that remain closed to the seer: Daniel is told that “the commands are covered and sealed,” and no one is found worthy to open John’s scroll. Daniel is told to go away, whereas John weeps.

findings.finding: 'Both present an object' misdescribes the Lamb.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both present an object with “seven eyes.” In Zechariah the eyes are on a stone set before Joshua; here they belong to the Lamb.
findings.after: Both speak of “seven eyes.” In Zechariah the eyes are on the stone set before Joshua; here they belong to the Lamb.

findings.finding: Revelation 5:8 does not place the incense before God’s throne; the elders fall before the Lamb.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both connect incense with “the prayers of the saints” offered before God’s throne. In Revelation 8:3–4 an angel offers it at the golden altar with a golden censer.
findings.after: Both connect incense with “the prayers of the saints.” In Revelation 8:3–4 an angel with a golden censer offers the incense with the prayers upon the golden altar before the throne.

findings.finding: The shown Psalm 39:4 does not mention deliverance.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both speak of singing “a new song” to God. In the Psalm it is put into the singer’s mouth after deliverance; here it is sung to the Lamb who was slaughtered.
findings.after: Both speak of singing “a new song” to God. In the Psalm it is put into the singer’s mouth as “a hymn to our God”; here it is sung to the Lamb who was slaughtered.

findings.finding: The shown Revelation 1:6 ascribes the glory to 'Him' without identifying Him; 'Christ alone' is not established by the shown text.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both doxologies ascribe “the glory and the dominion for the ages of the ages.” In Revelation 1:6 they are ascribed to Christ alone.
findings.after: Both doxologies ascribe “the glory and the dominion for the ages of the ages.” In Revelation 1:6 they are ascribed to a single “Him”; here to the One sitting upon the throne and to the Lamb.

findings.finding: In 5:14 only the living creatures say 'Amen'; the elders do not.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both show the four living creatures and the elders responding with “Amen” as the elders fall and worship; Revelation 19:4 adds “Hallelujah.”
findings.after: Both show the living creatures saying “Amen” and the elders falling to worship. In Revelation 19:4 the elders and the living creatures together fall, worship and say “Amen, Hallelujah!”

findings.finding: In Zechariah the white horses go out behind the black ones; it is the gray ones that travel around the earth. Revelation 6:2 shows a single white horse, not horses of other colours.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both visions include “white horses” that go out across the earth among horses of other colours. In Zechariah the horses draw chariots and are identified as the four winds of heaven.
findings.after: Both visions include white horses that go out: in Zechariah “the white ones were going out,” and John’s rider on a white horse “went out conquering.” In Zechariah the horses draw chariots and are identified as the four winds of heaven.

findings.finding: Neither shown text says the horses are 'sent out by God'.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both visions include red horses among horses of several colours sent out by God: Zechariah’s first chariot “had flame-red horses,” and John sees a horse “fiery red.”
findings.after: Both visions include red horses among horses of other colours: Zechariah’s first chariot “had flame-red horses,” and John sees “another horse” go out, “fiery red.”

findings.finding: 'Division' is not in the shown Matthew 10:34.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both pair the removal of peace on the earth with a sword: Jesus did not come “to bring peace upon the earth… but a sword,” and the rider is given “to take peace from the earth” and “a great sword.” Jesus speaks of division his coming brings, not of mutual slaughter.
findings.after: Both pair the removal of peace on the earth with a sword: Jesus did not come “to bring peace upon the earth… but a sword,” and the rider is given “to take peace from the earth” and “a great sword.” Jesus speaks of the purpose of his coming, not of mutual slaughter.

findings.finding: Revelation 6:10 calls the Master 'holy and true'; it does not describe God’s judging as true.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: The martyrs ask when God will “judge and avenge our blood”; Revelation 19:2 declares that He “judged the great prostitute” and “avenged the blood of His slaves.” Both also describe God's judging as “true.”
findings.after: The martyrs ask when God will “judge and avenge our blood”; Revelation 19:2 declares that He “judged the great prostitute” and “avenged the blood of His slaves.” The martyrs address the Master as “holy and true,” and 19:2 calls His judgments “true and righteous.”

findings.finding: Neither shown text locates the appeal 'in heaven', and Zechariah’s appeal does not open with 'how long'.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both open an appeal to God in heaven with the question “how long,” addressed to a sovereign title (“Lord Almighty”; “O Master”). Zechariah's angel asks about mercy for Jerusalem, whereas the martyrs ask for judgment and vengeance.
findings.after: Both appeal to God with the question “how long,” using a sovereign title (“Lord Almighty”; “O Master”). Zechariah’s angel asks about mercy for Jerusalem and Judah’s cities, whereas the martyrs ask for judgment and vengeance.

findings.finding: The shown Isaiah 2:19 says 'carrying them into caves', not that people go into caves themselves.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Isaiah describes people going “into caves, into clefts in the rocks” from the Lord's terror when He rises to shatter the earth. Revelation shows the kings and all classes hiding “in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains.”
findings.after: Isaiah speaks of carrying things “into caves, into clefts in the rocks” from the Lord’s terror when He rises to shatter the earth. Revelation shows the kings and people of every rank hiding themselves “in the caves and among the rocks of the mountains.”

findings.finding: Hosea has no 'hide us', and Revelation reworks rather than quotes Hosea’s cry, so 'quotation' and 'repeats the cry' overstate the relationship.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Hosea has the people say to the mountains “Cover us!” and to the hills “Fall upon us!” Revelation repeats the cry “Fall upon us and hide us” addressed to the mountains and rocks, adding hiding from the face of the One on the throne and the Lamb's wrath.
findings.after: Hosea has the people say to the mountains “Cover us!” and to the hills “Fall upon us!” Revelation adapts the cry as “Fall upon us and hide us,” addressed to the mountains and rocks, adding hiding from the face of the One on the throne and from the Lamb’s wrath.

findings.finding: Revelation 7:1 does not mention God’s slaves or the sealing.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Jesus says His angels will gather the chosen “from the four winds,” and Revelation pairs angels with the four winds in connection with God's slaves. In Matthew the angels gather; here they restrain the winds until the sealing.
findings.after: Jesus says His angels will gather the chosen “from the four winds,” and Revelation shows four angels holding “the four winds of the earth.” In Matthew the angels gather the chosen; here they hold back the winds.

findings.finding: The shown Ezekiel 9:4 does not say the marking happens 'before judgment falls'.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: In Ezekiel a man is sent to “put the sign upon the foreheads” of the faithful before judgment falls, as the angels here seal God's slaves “upon their foreheads” before harm is done. Ezekiel speaks of a sign, Revelation of a seal.
findings.after: In Ezekiel a man is told to “put the sign upon the foreheads” of those who grieve over the lawlessness in Jerusalem, as the angels here seal God’s slaves “upon their foreheads” before harm is done. Ezekiel speaks of a sign, Revelation of a seal.

findings.finding: The hundred forty-four thousand are not mentioned in Revelation 7:3, so they cannot 'reappear' from this verse.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: The hundred forty-four thousand reappear with the Lamb on Mount Zion, having His name and His Father's name “written upon their foreheads,” which corresponds to the sealing on the forehead here.
findings.after: The slaves of God sealed “upon their foreheads” here correspond to the hundred forty-four thousand with the Lamb on Mount Zion, who have His name and His Father’s name “written upon their foreheads.”

findings.finding: In 5:11–12 the angels are 'saying with a loud voice', not singing.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Revelation 5:11 shows “many angels around the throne and the living creatures and the elders,” the same arrangement given here. In chapter 5 the angels sing; here they fall on their faces and worship.
findings.after: Revelation 5:11 shows “many angels around the throne and the living creatures and the elders,” the same arrangement given here. In chapter 5 the angels acclaim the Lamb with a loud voice; here they fall on their faces and worship.

findings.finding: The shown Jeremiah 28:25 does not name an enemy power; it addresses a 'ruined mountain that ruins the whole earth'.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: God threatens to make the destroying mountain “like a burned mountain” and roll it down. Revelation sees “something like a great mountain burning with fire” thrown into the sea; Jeremiah's oracle concerns a named enemy power, not the sea.
findings.after: God threatens to roll the destroying mountain down from the rocks and make it “like a burned mountain.” Revelation sees “something like a great mountain burning with fire” thrown into the sea; Jeremiah’s oracle addresses a “ruined mountain that ruins the whole earth” and does not mention the sea.

findings.finding: The claim that the seer reports a number he 'did not see' is not stated in either text (in 9:17 he does see the horses). Also 9:16 reads 'I heard their number', not 'I heard the number'.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: In both verses the seer reports a number he did not see but heard: “I heard the number”. Revelation 7:4 gives the number of those sealed; 9:16 the number of the cavalry.
findings.after: In both verses the seer reports a number he heard: “I heard the number” in 7:4 and “I heard their number” in 9:16. Revelation 7:4 gives the number of those sealed; 9:16 the number of the cavalry.

findings.finding: 'Both angels are linked with a scroll' is not true of the shown source: Revelation 10:1 does not mention a scroll (the little scroll is in 10:2).
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Revelation 10:1 introduces “another mighty angel”, which recalls the “mighty angel” of 5:2. Both angels are linked with a scroll.
findings.after: Revelation 10:1 introduces “another mighty angel”, which recalls the “mighty angel” of 5:2 who asks who is worthy to open the scroll.

findings.finding: 'Both scrolls are later given to the seer to eat' is presented as part of these passages, but neither Ezekiel 2:9–10 nor Revelation 10:2 mentions eating.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: In Ezekiel a hand holds out “a scroll of a book” and unrolls it before the prophet; Revelation’s angel holds “a little scroll opened”. Both scrolls are later given to the seer to eat.
findings.after: In Ezekiel a hand holds out “a scroll of a book” and unrolls it before the prophet; Revelation’s angel holds “a little scroll opened”. Ezekiel’s scroll is written on the back and the front.

findings.finding: 'In both, the roar comes before divine speech' overstates the texts: Amos sets the lion's roar beside the Lord's speaking rather than before it, and Revelation does not call the seven thunders divine speech.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Amos 3:8 sets a lion’s roar beside the Lord’s speaking, and Revelation 10:3 compares the angel’s loud cry to a lion that roars. In both, the roar comes before divine speech: prophecy in Amos, the seven thunders in Revelation.
findings.after: Amos 3:8 sets a lion’s roar beside the Lord’s speaking, and Revelation 10:3 compares the angel’s loud cry to a lion that roars. In Revelation the cry is followed by the seven thunders speaking their own voices.

findings.finding: Says both figures 'swear by the One who lives for ever about when the end will come', but the shown source (Revelation 10:5) contains no oath; only the raised hand is in the source verse.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both figures raise a hand “to heaven” and swear by the One who lives for ever about when the end will come. Daniel’s figure raises both right and left hands; Revelation’s angel raises his right hand.
findings.after: Daniel’s figure raises his hands “to heaven” and swears by God who lives for ever; Revelation’s angel, standing upon the sea and upon the earth, raises his right hand “to heaven”. Daniel’s figure raises both right and left hands.

findings.finding: Ezekiel 2:8 as shown does not mention a scroll; the claim that this command 'leads to his eating the scroll' goes beyond the shown target.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Ezekiel 2:8 tells the prophet to “Open your mouth wide and eat what I give you”. This is the command that leads to his eating the scroll, which Revelation 10:9 echoes in “Take and devour it”.
findings.after: Ezekiel 2:8 tells the prophet to “Open your mouth wide and eat what I give you”. In Revelation 10:9 the angel tells the seer, of the little scroll, “Take and devour it”.

findings.finding: Claims 11:9 uses 'the same group of terms' as 10:11, but the lists differ: 11:9 has peoples, tribes, tongues, nations; 10:11 has peoples, nations, tongues, many kings.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Revelation 11:9 uses the same group of terms as 10:11, “the peoples and tribes and tongues and nations”, for those who look on the dead witnesses.
findings.after: Revelation 11:9 uses a similar group of terms, “the peoples and tribes and tongues and nations”, for those who look on the dead bodies; 10:11 has “peoples and nations and tongues and many kings”.

findings.finding: Says Daniel 7:25 hands 'the holy ones of the Most High into the oppressor’s power', but the shown text says 'Everything will be handed into his hands'. The holy ones are 'worn down', not said to be handed over. 'Shared image' also fits a shared time period poorly.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Daniel 7:25 hands the holy ones of the Most High into the oppressor’s power “for a time, times, and half a time”. Revelation 11:2 gives a set period for the holy city to be trampled. Neither text states that the two periods are equal.
findings.after: In Daniel 7:25 the one who will “wear down the holy ones of the Most High” has everything handed into his hands “for a time, times, and half a time”. Revelation 11:2 gives a set period, forty-two months, for the nations to trample the holy city. Neither text states that the two periods are equal.

findings.finding: The label 'quotation' does not fit. Revelation’s wording ('the two olive trees and the two lampstands standing before the Lord of the earth') adapts Zechariah and does not reproduce it; the rationale itself describes an allusion.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Zechariah asks about “these two olive trees” and is told that they “stand beside the Lord of all the earth”. Revelation 11:4 calls the witnesses “the two olive trees” “standing before the Lord of the earth”.
findings.after: Zechariah asks about “these two olive trees” and is told that they “stand beside the Lord of all the earth”. Revelation 11:4 calls the witnesses “the two olive trees” “standing before the Lord of the earth”.

findings.finding: 'while Elisha looks on' and 'in sight of others' are not in the shown 2 Kings 2:11, which names neither Elisha nor any onlookers.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Elijah is “taken up … as into heaven” while Elisha looks on, and the witnesses likewise go up into heaven in sight of others. Elijah is taken up in a tumult, with a chariot of fire, rather than in a cloud.
findings.after: Elijah is “taken up … as into heaven”, and the witnesses likewise go up into heaven. Elijah is taken up in a tumult, with a chariot of fire, rather than in a cloud, and the shown text does not mention onlookers as Revelation does.

findings.finding: 'in response to a heavenly announcement' is not in the shown Revelation 19:4.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Revelation 19:4 likewise says that “the twenty-four elders … fell and worshipped God”, in response to a heavenly announcement.
findings.after: Revelation 19:4 likewise says that “the twenty-four elders … fell and worshipped God”, here God “who sitteth upon the throne”.

findings.finding: Says the holy ones are 'handed over' to the persecuting figure for that period, but the shown Daniel 7:25 says 'Everything will be handed into his hands'; the holy ones are 'worn down'.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Daniel gives the same period, “a time, times, and half a time,” for which the holy ones are handed over to the persecuting figure. Revelation uses it for the time the woman is nourished away from the serpent.
findings.after: Daniel gives the same period, “a time, times, and half a time”, for which everything is handed into the hands of the one who wears down the holy ones of the Most High. Revelation uses it for the time the woman is nourished away from the serpent.

findings.finding: The quoted formula “every tribe and … tongue and people and nation” follows the order of 5:9 only; 13:7 reads “every tribe and people and tongue and nation”, so the quotation is not true of both verses.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both use the fourfold formula “every tribe and … tongue and people and nation.” In 5:9 the Lamb purchases people from them for God; in 13:7 the beast receives authority over them.
findings.after: Both use the fourfold formula of tribe, people, tongue and nation: 5:9 has “every tribe and tongue and people and nation,” and 13:7 has “every tribe and people and tongue and nation.” In 5:9 the Lamb purchases people from them for God; in 13:7 the beast receives authority over them.

findings.finding: The rationale calls the first harvest one “of grain”; 14:15–16 speaks only of “the harvest of the earth” and does not name grain.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Revelation 14:15–16 has the same pattern: an angel cries “with a loud voice” to the one with the sickle, “Send Thy sickle and reap,” and the earth is reaped. The first harvest is of grain; the second is of the vine.
findings.after: Revelation 14:15–16 has the same pattern: an angel cries “with a loud voice” to the one with the sickle, “Send Thy sickle and reap,” and the earth is reaped. The first is a reaping of “the harvest of the earth”; the second is a gathering of “the clusters of the vine of the earth.”

findings.finding: The label “quotation” overstates the link: Revelation reorders the psalm’s words and has “worship” for “bow down”, with no citation formula. The rationale itself says “closely reproduces”, so the right label is verbal allusion.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: The psalm says, “All the nations Thou madest will come and bow down before Thee, Lord, and glorify Thy name,” which the song closely reproduces: “glorify Thy name … all the nations shall come and worship before Thee.”
findings.after: The psalm says, “All the nations Thou madest will come and bow down before Thee, Lord, and glorify Thy name,” which the song closely reproduces: “glorify Thy name … all the nations shall come and worship before Thee.”

findings.finding: 21:9 does not show that the angel shows the bride or that the hearer is John; the angel says “Come, I will show thee the bride,” speaking to “me.”
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both verses speak of the seven angels with seven bowls full of judgement: here “seven golden bowls full of the fury of God,” there “the seven bowls full of the seven last plagues.” In 21:9 one of these angels shows John the bride.
findings.after: Both verses speak of the seven angels with seven bowls full of judgement: here “seven golden bowls full of the fury of God,” there “the seven bowls full of the seven last plagues.” In 21:9 one of these angels says to the seer, “Come, I will show thee the bride, the wife of the Lamb.”

findings.finding: Isaiah 6:4 as shown does not link the smoke to the cry: the cry lifts the lintel, and the house being filled with smoke is a separate clause. “Seraphim” is also not named in the shown text.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: In both visions the sanctuary is filled with smoke: “the house was filled with smoke” and “the temple was filled with smoke.” Isaiah links the smoke to the seraphim’s cry, while Revelation links it to the glory and power of God.
findings.after: In both visions the sanctuary is filled with smoke: “the house was filled with smoke” and “the temple was filled with smoke.” In Isaiah this happens as the lintel is lifted “at the sound of their cry,” while Revelation says the smoke comes “from the glory of God and from His power.”

findings.finding: The quoted phrase “who is coming” appears in neither verse shown; the rationale draws on 1:4, 1:8 and 4:8, which are not part of this pair. “The elders” are also not named in 11:17 as shown.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both address God as “the One who is and who was” without the further phrase “who is coming” used in 1:4, 1:8 and 4:8. In 11:17 the elders give thanks for His reign; here the angel praises His judgment.
findings.after: Both address God as “the One who is and who was.” In 11:17 the speakers give thanks because He has taken His great power and reigned; here the angel of the waters declares Him righteous because He judged “these things.”

findings.finding: Rationale says Revelation's hail falls on God's 'enemies' 'with deadly effect' and that God sends it; Rev 16:21 says only that hail comes down from heaven upon people, who blaspheme God, and mentions no deaths.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: In both, God sends hail “from heaven” upon His enemies with deadly effect. In Joshua the hail falls on fleeing armies; in Revelation the hail, about a talent in weight, falls on people who then blaspheme God.
findings.after: In both, hail comes down “from heaven” in judgment. In Joshua the Lord hurls hailstones from heaven on the fleeing armies, and more die from the hailstones than by the sword; in Revelation great hail, about a talent in weight, comes down from heaven upon people, who then blaspheme God because of the plague of hail.

findings.finding: Label 'quotation' overstates it: Revelation's wording ('I sit a queen, and I am not a widow') is a close echo, not a quotation of Isaiah's 'I will not sit as a widow or know bereavement.' Rationale is otherwise accurate.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Babylon’s boast in Isaiah, “I will not sit as a widow or know bereavement,” spoken “in her heart,” is closely echoed: “in her heart she saith, ‘I sit a queen, and I am not a widow.’” Isaiah adds that widowhood and childlessness will come “in one day.”
findings.after: Babylon’s boast in Isaiah, “I will not sit as a widow or know bereavement,” spoken “in her heart,” is closely echoed: “in her heart she saith, ‘I sit a queen, and I am not a widow.’” Isaiah adds that widowhood and childlessness will come “in one day.”

findings.finding: Wrong agent: in the shown text Jeremiah instructs the addressee ('When you finish reading this scroll, bind a stone to it and throw it'); Jeremiah does not throw the stone himself. Label 'symbolic act fulfilled' is also inaccurate: Revelation repeats a parallel sign rather than fulfilling Jeremiah's act.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: In both passages a stone is thrown into water as a sign of Babylon’s end: Jeremiah binds a stone to a scroll and throws it into the Euphrates, saying “Thus Babylon will sink and certainly not rise.” Revelation’s mighty angel throws a millstone into the sea, saying “In this way Babylon the great city will be thrown.”
findings.after: In both passages a stone is thrown into water as a sign of Babylon’s end: the one addressed in Jeremiah is told to bind a stone to the scroll and throw it into the Euphrates, saying “Thus Babylon will sink and certainly not rise.” Revelation’s mighty angel throws a stone like a great millstone into the sea, saying “In this way Babylon the great city will be thrown.”

findings.finding: Rationale says 'God will end' the musicians, but the shown Ezekiel text has an unidentified third person ('He will put an end'), who in context is the conquering king, not God.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Ezekiel says of Tyre that God will end “the multitude of your musicians” and that “the sound of your psalteries will certainly no longer be heard,” matching Revelation’s musicians whose sound “will certainly not be heard in thee any more.”
findings.after: Ezekiel says of Tyre, “He will put an end to the multitude of your musicians, and the sound of your psalteries will certainly no longer be heard,” matching Revelation’s musicians whose sound “will certainly not be heard in thee any more.”

findings.finding: Rationale calls all Jeremiah's items 'sounds' (the light of a lamp is not a sound) and says 'the same items' follow in Rev 18:22–23, though the sound of joy is not there and the bridegroom/bride and lamp are in 18:23, not the source verse 18:22.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Jeremiah lists sounds removed in judgment, including the sound of joy, “the sound of bridegroom and bride” and “the light of a lamp,” the same items that follow in Revelation 18:22–23. Jeremiah’s list in this reading has “the fragrance of ointment” and no mill.
findings.after: Jeremiah’s judgment removes “the sound of joy and delight,” as Revelation’s city will no longer hear the sound of its musicians. Jeremiah’s list goes on to “the sound of bridegroom and bride” and “the light of a lamp,” which Revelation takes up in the next verse (18:23). In this reading Jeremiah has “the fragrance of ointment” and no mill.

findings.finding: Misleading splice: the quoted 'selling nations … through her potions' joins two clauses; Nahum says 'selling nations through her prostitution and tribes through her potions.'
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Nahum’s city is a prostitute and “mistress of potions, selling nations … through her potions,” as Babylon deceived “all the nations” by her sorcery. Nahum addresses Nineveh rather than Babylon.
findings.after: Nahum’s city is a prostitute and “mistress of potions,” “selling nations through her prostitution and tribes through her potions,” as Babylon deceived “all the nations” by her sorcery. Nahum addresses Nineveh rather than Babylon.

findings.finding: Misquotation: 'the voice of bridegroom and the voice of bride' is Jeremiah's wording only; Revelation has 'the voice of bridegroom and bride.'
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both oracles of judgment end “the voice of bridegroom and the voice of bride” in the city. Jeremiah applies this to Judah’s cities and Jerusalem; Revelation applies it to Babylon.
findings.after: Both oracles of judgment silence the voice of bridegroom and bride: Jeremiah will stop “the voice of bridegroom and the voice of bride,” and in Revelation “the voice of bridegroom and bride will certainly not be heard in thee any more.” Jeremiah applies this to Judah’s cities and Jerusalem; Revelation applies it to Babylon.

findings.finding: The psalm's 'Let peoples be angry' is not a statement that the proclamation is 'in response to His rule over the peoples'; that clause misreads the target.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: The psalm proclaims “The Lord has become King!” in response to His rule over the peoples, which corresponds to the Hallelujah because God “hath reigned.”
findings.after: The psalm proclaims “The Lord has become King!”, as the multitude cries “Hallelujah, because the Lord God Almighty hath reigned.”

findings.finding: Label 'same title' overstates it: 1 Timothy's 'the King of those who reign and Lord of those who rule' differs in wording from 'King of kings and Lord of lords' (the parallel pair P747 is labelled 'parallel title').
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Paul calls God “the King of those who reign and Lord of those who rule,” which corresponds to the paired title “King of kings and Lord of lords.”
findings.after: Paul calls God “the King of those who reign and Lord of those who rule,” which corresponds to the paired title “King of kings and Lord of lords.” The wording differs.

findings.finding: The rationale quotes 'the lake burning with fire and sulfur' as wording of both verses, but 19:20 reads 'the lake of fire burning with sulfur'.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both verses name “the lake burning with fire and sulfur.” Revelation 21:8 assigns it to the unbelieving and other sinners and identifies it as “the second death.”
findings.after: Revelation 19:20 speaks of “the lake of fire burning with sulfur” and 21:8 of “the lake burning with fire and sulfur.” Revelation 21:8 assigns it to the unbelieving and other sinners and identifies it as “the second death.”

findings.finding: Says the angel in 20:1 uses the key to shut the dragon in; the shutting is in 20:3, not in the shown source. 9:1 also reads 'the key of the shaft of the abyss'.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: In both visions a figure from heaven holds “the key” of the abyss. In 9:1 it is given to a fallen star who opens the shaft; in 20:1 an angel uses it to shut the dragon in.
findings.after: In 20:1 an angel coming down from heaven has “the key of the abyss”; in 9:1 “the key of the shaft of the abyss” is given to a star fallen from heaven, who opens the shaft.

findings.finding: Attributes binding the dragon and Satan's thousand-year binding to 20:1, which only mentions the angel with the key and a great chain.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Jude says God keeps rebellious angels “in everlasting chains under gloom for the judgment,” as the angel comes with “a great chain” to bind the dragon. Jude speaks of angels kept until judgment; Revelation of Satan bound for a thousand years.
findings.after: Jude says God keeps the angels who abandoned their proper dwelling “in everlasting chains under gloom for the judgment of the great day,” and in 20:1 an angel comes down from heaven with the key of the abyss and “a great chain” upon his hand.

findings.finding: 'They wait under the altar' is an interpretation; 6:9 only says the souls were seen beneath the altar.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both verses speak of the souls of those killed “because of the word of God” and because of their testimony. In 6:9 they wait under the altar; in 20:4 they live and reign.
findings.after: Both verses speak of the souls of those killed “because of the word of God” and because of their testimony. In 6:9 they are seen beneath the altar; in 20:4 they live and reign with Christ.

findings.finding: Identifies the foreigners as Philistines; the shown text of 1 Samuel 13:5 says only 'the foreigners'.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: The foreigners “gathered for war” with people “as numerous as the sand by the sea,” as Satan gathers the nations for war, “whose number is like the sand of the sea.” Samuel narrates a Philistine muster against Israel.
findings.after: The foreigners “gathered for war” against Israel with people “as numerous as the sand by the sea,” as Satan gathers the nations for war, “whose number is like the sand of the sea.” Samuel narrates a muster of the foreigners against Israel.

findings.finding: Calls those in 7:17 'the multitude'; the shown verse speaks only of 'them' whom the Lamb shepherds.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both say that God will wipe every tear from their eyes. In Revelation 7:17 this is said of the multitude shepherded by the Lamb, and here of those with whom God dwells in the new creation.
findings.after: Both say that God will wipe every tear from their eyes. In Revelation 7:17 this is said of those whom the Lamb shepherds and guides to springs of waters of life, and here of those with whom God dwells.

findings.finding: Says Ezekiel is brought to the temple gate; the shown verse says 'the entrance of the inner gate facing north' and does not mention the temple.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: In Ezekiel a spirit lifts the prophet and brings him “to Jerusalem in a vision of God”. Here John is carried away in the Spirit and shown the holy city Jerusalem. Ezekiel is brought to the existing temple gate rather than shown a city descending.
findings.after: In Ezekiel a spirit lifts the prophet and brings him “to Jerusalem in a vision of God”. Here John is carried away in the Spirit and shown the holy city Jerusalem. Ezekiel is brought to the entrance of the inner gate facing north rather than shown a city descending.

findings.finding: Says the glory comes to the temple; Ezekiel 43:2 as shown says only that it came 'by the way of the gate facing east'.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Ezekiel sees “the glory of the God of Israel” coming, with the earth flashing “like radiance from the glory”. The city likewise has “the glory of God” and a radiance. Ezekiel’s glory comes to the temple by the east gate.
findings.after: Ezekiel sees “the glory of the God of Israel” coming, with the earth flashing “like radiance from the glory”. The city likewise has “the glory of God” and a radiance. In Ezekiel the glory comes by the way of the gate facing east.

findings.finding: Names Abraham, who is not named in the shown Hebrews 11:10.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Hebrews describes Abraham awaiting “the city that has foundations, whose craftsman and maker is God.” Revelation describes the foundations of the city that comes down from God.
findings.after: Hebrews says “he was awaiting the city that has foundations, whose craftsman and maker is God.” Revelation describes the twelve foundations of the city's wall.

findings.finding: 'In a vision' is not stated in the shown Ezekiel 41:1–5.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: In Ezekiel a guide measures the temple’s doorways and wall in a vision, and here an angel measures the city’s gates and wall. Ezekiel’s measurements concern the temple, not a city.
findings.after: In Ezekiel a guide measures the temple's porch, doorways and wall, and here the one speaking with John has a reed to measure the city's gates and wall. Ezekiel's measurements concern the temple, not a city.

findings.finding: Claims both visions 'end' with the city's measurement; Revelation 21:16 is not the end of John's vision.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both visions end by giving the measurement of the city: Ezekiel’s circuit is “eighteen thousand”, and Revelation’s city is twelve thousand stadia. The figures and units differ, and the verse in Ezekiel does not say the city is foursquare.
findings.after: Both give a measurement of the whole city: Ezekiel's circuit is “eighteen thousand”, and Revelation's city is twelve thousand stadia. The figures and units differ, and the verse in Ezekiel does not say the city is foursquare.

findings.finding: Says Isaiah addresses 'the city'; the shown text addresses a 'Humbled and unsettled woman'.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Isaiah promises the city “sapphire as your foundations” and “battlements jasper”, and Revelation names jasper and sapphire as the first two foundations. Isaiah lists fewer stones and assigns jasper to the battlements.
findings.after: Isaiah promises the afflicted woman “sapphire as your foundations” and “battlements jasper”, and Revelation names jasper and sapphire as the first two foundations of the city's wall. Isaiah lists fewer stones and assigns jasper to the battlements.

findings.finding: Refers to the high priest's breastpiece; the shown Exodus text mentions only 'a fabric set with four rows of stones', not the high priest or a breastpiece.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: The high priest’s breastpiece has four rows of stones, including sapphire, jasper and emerald, each bearing a name of the twelve tribes. Revelation’s twelve foundations are adorned with stones and bear the apostles’ names. The two stone lists overlap only in part.
findings.after: Exodus prescribes a fabric set with four rows of stones, including sapphire, jasper and emerald, bearing the names of the twelve tribes. Revelation's foundations are adorned with precious stones, the first four being jasper, sapphire, chalcedony and emerald. The two stone lists overlap only in part.

findings.finding: Calls the fabric 'priestly'; the shown Exodus text does not mention a priest.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Five of the stones named for these foundations also appear in the four rows of stones woven into the priestly fabric in Exodus: “sardius,” “topaz,” “chrysolite,” “beryl” and “amethyst.” The two lists differ in order and in their other stones.
findings.after: Five of the stones named for these foundations also appear in the four rows of stones woven into the fabric in Exodus: “sardius,” “topaz,” “chrysolite,” “beryl” and “amethyst.” The two lists differ in order and in their other stones.

findings.finding: Names Zion as the addressee; the shown Isaiah 60:16 does not mention Zion.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Isaiah says Zion will “suck the nations’ milk and eat kings’ wealth”, and Revelation says nations walk by the city’s light and kings bring their glory into it. Isaiah speaks of wealth received rather than glory brought.
findings.after: Isaiah tells the one addressed, “You will suck the nations' milk and eat kings' wealth”, and Revelation says nations walk by the city's light and kings bring their glory into it. Isaiah speaks of wealth received rather than glory brought.

findings.finding: Says those in 13:8 worship 'the beast'; the shown verse says only 'worship it'.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both refer to the book of life belonging to the Lamb. In Revelation 13:8 those not written in it worship the beast, and here only those written in it enter the city.
findings.after: Both refer to the book of life belonging to the Lamb. In Revelation 13:8 those whose names are not written in it worship “it”, and here only those written in it enter the city.

findings.finding: Says the river flows 'in the city'; the shown 22:1 says only that it comes out of the throne of God and of the Lamb.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Zechariah sees “living water” going out from Jerusalem, and John sees the river of water of life flowing in the city from the throne. Zechariah’s water flows to the first and last seas.
findings.after: Zechariah sees “living water” going out from Jerusalem, and John is shown a river of water of life coming out of the throne of God and of the Lamb. Zechariah's water flows to the first and last seas.

findings.finding: Says Revelation places the river 'in the city of God'; the shown 22:1 does not mention the city.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: The psalm speaks of a river whose streams “gladden God’s city”. Revelation places a river of water of life in the city of God.
findings.after: The psalm speaks of a river whose streams “gladden God's city”, and Revelation shows a river of water of life coming out of the throne of God and of the Lamb.

findings.finding: Says the angel forbids the worship 'in both places'; the prohibition is in 19:10 but not in the shown 22:8 (it comes in 22:9).
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Both describe John falling before the angel’s feet to worship. Revelation 19:10 records the same scene earlier in the book, and in both places the angel forbids it.
findings.after: Both describe John falling before the feet of the one showing him the visions in order to worship. Revelation 19:10 records the same act earlier in the book, where the angel forbids it.

findings.finding: The final sentence ('Both appear after the end-time words...') is vague and not supported by the shown texts.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Daniel says that “many are tested and made holy, and sinners sin”, which Revelation echoes in letting the wrongdoer still do wrong and the holy one still be sanctified. Both appear after the end-time words in Daniel and in Revelation.
findings.after: Daniel says that “many are tested and made holy, and sinners sin”, which Revelation echoes in letting the wrongdoer still do wrong and the holy one still be sanctified.

findings.finding: Claims Ezekiel has the same 'let … still' form, but 'still' does not occur in Ezekiel 3:27; the house is called 'embittering', not 'rebellious'.
findings.resolution: Rationale/relationship replaced with the reader’s corrected wording.
findings.before: Ezekiel’s “Let the one who hears hear, and let the one who disobeys disobey” has the same paired “let … still” form. Ezekiel says it of a rebellious house hearing the prophet.
findings.after: Ezekiel's “Let the one who hears hear, and let the one who disobeys disobey” has the same paired “let the one who … ” form as Revelation's sayings. Ezekiel is to say it to an “embittering house.”

rejected_pairs.finding: Ezekiel 2:10 as shown says nothing about eating the scroll, sweetness or the mouth; 'the scroll Ezekiel is given to eat' and 'set beside the sweetness in the mouth' come from outside the shown verse. The only remaining link to Revelation 10:10 (bitterness) is an inference from 'a lament, a song and woe'. The rationale admits that Ezekiel does not speak of bitterness, so no specific connection remains.
